Anterior gradient 2 (AGR2) is a cancer-associated secreted protein found predominantly in adenocarcinomas. Given its ubiquity in solid tumors, cancer-secreted AGR2 could be a useful biomarker in urine or blood for early detection. However, normal organs express and might also secrete AGR2, which would impact its utility as a cancer biomarker. Uniform AGR2 expression is found in the normal bladder urothelium. Little AGR2 is secreted by the urothelial cells as no measurable amounts could be detected in urine. The urinary proteomes of healthy people contain no listing for AGR2. Likewise, the blood proteomes of healthy people also contain no significant peptide counts for AGR2 suggesting little urothelial secretion into capillaries of the lamina propria. Expression of AGR2 is lost in urothelial carcinoma, with only 25% of primary tumors observed to retain AGR2 expression in a cohort of lymph node-positive cases. AGR2 is secreted by the urothelial carcinoma cells as urinary AGR2 was measured in the voided urine of 25% of the cases analyzed in a cohort of cancer vs . non-cancer patients. The fraction of AGR2-positive urine samples was consistent with the fraction of urothelial carcinoma that stained positive for AGR2. Since cancer cells secrete AGR2 while normal cells do not, its measurement in body fluids could be used to indicate tumor presence. Furthermore, AGR2 has also been found on the cell surface of cancer cells. Taken together, secretion and cell surface localization of AGR2 are characteristic of cancer, while expression of AGR2 by itself is not. secreted AGR2 bladder cancer subcellular localization urine biomarker INTRODUCTION Anterior gradient 2 (AGR2) is an adenocarcinoma antigen with elevated expression in many solid tumor types including prostate, breast, pancreatic, gastro-intestinal, lung. The protein is a protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) found in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) where it functions as a molecular chaperone in protein folding [ 1 ]. The ER could have an important role in carcinogenesis and tumor biology [ 2 ]. A non-canonic ER retention motif ( C -terminal KTEL) in AGR2 may be responsible for the diverse trafficking of this molecule [ 3 ]. In addition to the ER, AGR2 can be shunted to the nucleus, cell surface or extracellular space. Secreted AGR2 can function to trigger cellular differentiation in responding cells as documented in salamander limb regeneration [ 4 ]. AGR2 is secreted as a 19 kDa protein by prostate cancer cells measurable at pg/ml levels in the urine [ 5 ], and blood [ 6 ] of patients. AGR2 was identified as a biomarker candidate in prostate cancer by comparative transcriptomic analysis of sorted CD26 + cancer cells vs . CD26 + luminal cells [ 7 ]. In this approach, genes with elevated expression encoding secreted proteins in cancer are considered to be viable candidates; genes expressed by both cancer and normal cell types are not, and are thus ignored. A further consideration is that AGR2 expressed in the cancer of one organ could be expressed in the normal tissue of other organs, which would impact its utility as a biomarker. There would be very few cancer-specific biomarkers based on expression difference if examined systematically between cancer and all normal tissue. This is not unexpected since every gene in the genome serves a useful function in some cell types. AGR2 is secreted by pancreatic cancer cells [ 8 ], and localized on the cell surface of pancreatic cancer cells [ 9 ]. Whether normal AGR2-positive cells also secrete or express this protein on the cell surface is not known. Both normal prostate and pancreatic epithelial cells do not express AGR2 [ 7 , 9 ]. In this study, urinary bladder expression of AGR2 was investigated. Cell-type transcriptomes previously indicated that CD9 + urothelial cells were positive for AGR2 expression [ 10 ]. The entire urothelium was immunostained positive for AGR2. However, AGR2 was not observed to be secreted by the urothelial cells as little of this protein was detected in urine [ 5 , 6 ]. This finding was supported by database query of urine proteomes containing urinary proteins identified by large-scale mass spectrometry proteomics. Database query of blood proteomes similarly indicated little AGR2 in circulation as, for example, from secretion by urothelial cells into capillaries within the underlying lamina propria. AGR2 expression is lost in urothelial carcinoma, but a minority of bladder tumors were found to retain AGR2. The detection of AGR2 in the urine of a subset of bladder cancer patients indicates that AGR2 could be secreted by urothelial carcinoma cells. The take home message is that differential subcellular localization or protein address of AGR2 – cell interior vs . cell exterior – not expression, makes AGR2 a cancer biomarker. This may reflect the different functional roles played by AGR2 in normal cells vs . cancer cells. Such localization differences appear to be a property of PDI enzymes [ 11 ]. Cell surface expression could be inhibited by Brefeldin A [ 12 ]. In clinical utility, AGR2 + cancer cells can be targeted for eradication by agents such as antibodies or antibody drug conjugates, while AGR2 + normal cells would be spared.

molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Cancer development and progression, particularly tumorigenesis, metastasis, and the role of cancer cell AGR2 overexpression and secretion in bladder and prostate cancer.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: AGR2 functions as a protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) and molecular chaperone in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). Its diverse trafficking to the nucleus, cell surface, or extracellular space, possibly due to a non-canonic ER retention motif (C-terminal KTEL) or saturation of KDEL receptors in cancer cells, leads to secretion. Differential subcellular localization (cell interior vs. cell exterior), specifically secretion and cell surface localization, not mere expression, defines AGR2 as a cancer biomarker. Secreted AGR2 can trigger cellular differentiation and induces programmed cell death in prostate stromal cells. AGR2 is secreted by prostate and bladder cancer cells but not by normal urothelial cells, despite being expressed by both cancer and normal cells. The molecular mechanism of AGR2 predominance in late-stage bladder cancer remains to be fully determined. AGR2 and CD10 appear to have contrasting roles in local versus distal tumor spread, with CD10 linked to lymph node metastasis in prostate cancer cells. Differential subcellular localization may also involve different AGR2 isoforms or post-translational modifications.

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: AGR2 is secreted at pg/ml levels in urine and blood of prostate cancer patients. AGR2 immunostaining showed higher intensity and 40 times higher expression in prostate cancer cells compared to normal bladder urothelium. In bladder cancer, staining for AGR2 appeared stronger than normal urothelial cells in many cases, with expression higher in primary tumor centers (24%) compared to invasion fronts (12%), and further increasing in lymph node metastases (44%). AGR2 expression correlates with tumor characteristics such as stage, extracapsular extension, and the number and total diameter of metastases. High serum AGR2 levels (ng/ml range) have been reported, though the reliability of some commercial ELISA assays using polyclonal antibodies is suspect.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: AGR2 secretion is specific to cancer cells, including bladder cancer cells, while normal bladder cells express but do not secrete AGR2. Little to no AGR2 is released into urine by the normal bladder or detected in normal urine/blood, making its presence in body fluids indicative of tumor presence. This differential secretion and cell surface localization (demonstrated by specific labeling of AGR2+ pancreatic tumors but not normal tissues by an anti-AGR2 antibody) are characteristic of cancer. While AGR2 expression can be down-regulated in most bladder cancer cells, an overall increase is observed in bladder tumors, and importantly, its secretion signifies malignancy. The study design also explicitly aimed to ensure specificity for bladder cancer by excluding patients with concurrent prostate cancer.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Bladder cancer patients (including those with lymph node involvement, n=152), prostate cancer patients, and healthy individuals (including young female donors and those providing benign bladder tissue) for comparative analysis.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: Measurement of secreted AGR2 in body fluids serves as a viable biomarker for early detection and indication of tumor presence in bladder cancer, with elevated urinary AGR2 levels associated with urothelial carcinoma. AGR2 is an attractive tumor-associated antigen for therapeutic targeting, as AGR2-positive cancer cells could be targeted for eradication by agents like antibodies or antibody-drug conjugates, while normal cells are spared. Malignant transformation in bladder cancer often involves a loss of urothelial AGR2 expression in primary tumors, yet AGR2 can be detected in lymph node metastases. AGR2 expression in bladder cancer correlates with tumor characteristics such as stage, extracapsular extension, and the extent of metastases, implying its role in prognosis and disease progression. AGR2-positive lymph nodes suggest a greater potential for local cancer spread. High levels of free AGR2 in circulation are hypothesized to have deleterious effects on normal tissue cells. Urinary AGR2 measurement is also a viable test for prostate cancer detection.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: AGR2 demonstrates significant diagnostic utility for bladder cancer, with urinary AGR2 showing an AUC of 0.73, and for prostate cancer detection. It is also identified as a therapeutic target. AGR2+ lymph nodes indicate an adverse risk for greater local cancer spread. While AGR2 expression in bladder tumors was not generally correlated with patient survival (P > 0.05), low or absent AGR2 staining in the primary tumor was, in some cases, associated with longer survival. The correlation of AGR2 expression with tumor stage and metastases implies its prognostic relevance, but the overall prognostic risk classification for bladder cancer requires further clarification due to mixed findings on survival correlation.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: AGR2 demonstrates high utility as a cancer biomarker due to its specific secretion by cancer cells, not by normal bladder cells, making its presence in body fluids a cancer-specific indicator. The consistency between AGR2-positive urine samples and urothelial carcinoma staining reinforces its reliability. While DNA microarray signals and immunostaining intensity show good correlation, and both polyclonal and monoclonal antibodies recognized similar cell types, there are concerns about the reliability of certain commercial ELISA assays for serum AGR2, particularly those using polyclonal antibodies that exhibited suspect specificity (detecting AGR2 where monoclonal antibodies and DNA arrays showed negativity). In contrast, targeted proteomics offers higher reliability due to its lack of cross-reactivity and unique peptide identification. AGR2 was not reliably detectable in normal urine via Western blotting or proteome database queries, although ELISA sometimes showed detectability in non-cancer samples, attributed to normal tissue turnover, but was consistently significant in cancer urine. The reliability of ELISA measurements was further assessed by ROC curves and AUC calculations.
recommended_alternatives: Monoclonal antibodies (preferred over polyclonal antibodies of suspect specificity)
Purification of AGR2 from cancer cells for comparison to normal tissue
Larger cohort studies (over 1,000 cases) for bladder cancer to resolve divergent conclusions
Harvesting tumor metastases in advanced diseases to study AGR2 expression in late stages
